questions.q: What are the four parts of every project write-up in this research lab?
options: Introduction, body, conclusion, references
Claim, method, result, limitation
Abstract, data, model, code
Hypothesis, experiment, data, discussion
questions.explain: Every write-up in the lab, including Project 3's, follows the same claim, method, result, limitation structure.

questions.q: Why should Project 3's claim say RLAIF-style rather than claiming equivalence to human feedback?
options: Because RLAIF trains faster than RLHF
Because the reward used is a programmatic execution-correctness check standing in for a human rater, not literal human feedback
Because RLAIF and RLHF are unrelated techniques
Because the claim section should never mention the reward
questions.explain: Being precise about RLAIF versus RLHF matters because the reward is computed, not rated by a human — overstating it as literal human feedback would misrepresent the method.

questions.q: What belongs in the method section of the write-up?
options: Only the final accuracy number
A reproducible description of the base model, SFT data and procedure, reward function, and RLHF setup
A list of unrelated papers
The write-up's limitation section
questions.explain: The method section should let someone reconstruct the pipeline: base model choice, SFT via LoRA, the execution-correctness reward, and the PPOTrainer RLHF run.

questions.q: Why shouldn't the write-up claim SQL Pete 'learned' to avoid destructive SQL statements?
options: Because SQL Pete can execute destructive statements freely
Because the safety rule filtered out non-SELECT statements before they ever reached the reward function, so the model never had the chance to try them
Because destructive statements were never part of the reward schedule
Because the model was never trained on any SQL at all
questions.explain: The safety rule is a hard pre-execution constraint, not a learned behavior — the model never had the opportunity to attempt and be penalized for a destructive statement.

questions.q: How should the hallucination finding from Lesson 19 be handled in the write-up, if RLHF did NOT increase hallucination?
options: It should be omitted since there's nothing to report
It should still be reported plainly — a clean negative result is still a result
The write-up should claim RLHF eliminated all hallucination forever
The finding should be moved to the claim section only
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a clean negative result (no hallucination regression found) should still be stated plainly in the limitation section, not hidden or omitted.
